:::{#exm-poisson-sample-sufficient}
#### Two Poisson samples with the same sum have a likelihood ratio free of the rate

<!-- no-figure: the example compares four ratios computed from two samples -->

By @thm-exponential-family-sufficient,
the sum of the counts is sufficient for the natural parameter of the
[Poisson distribution](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/distributions.html#def-poisson).
So two samples with the same sum differ in their joint mass functions
only by a factor that does not depend on the parameter.
To check this on data,
we take the first three cyclone counts of @exm-poisson-exponential-family, 6, 5 and 4,
and the three equal counts 5, 5 and 5.
Both samples sum to 15.
We compute the ratio of their joint mass functions at four values of the rate $\rate$.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

##### R

```{r}
#| label: poisson-sample-sufficient-r
#| code-fold: false
sample_a <- c(6, 5, 4)
sample_b <- c(5, 5, 5)

joint_mass <- function(x, rate) {
  masses <- dpois(x, rate)
  prod(masses)
}

rates <- c(2, 4, 6, 8)
masses_a <- purrr::map_dbl(rates, \(r) joint_mass(sample_a, r))
masses_b <- purrr::map_dbl(rates, \(r) joint_mass(sample_b, r))
ratio <- masses_a / masses_b

tibble::tibble(rates, masses_a, masses_b, ratio)
```

##### Python

```{python}
#| label: poisson-sample-sufficient-py
#| code-fold: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import poisson

sample_a = np.array([6, 5, 4])
sample_b = np.array([5, 5, 5])

rates = np.array([2, 4, 6, 8])
masses_a = [np.prod(poisson.pmf(sample_a, r)) for r in rates]
masses_b = [np.prod(poisson.pmf(sample_b, r)) for r in rates]
ratio = np.array(masses_a) / np.array(masses_b)

pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "rates": rates,
        "masses_a": masses_a,
        "masses_b": masses_b,
        "ratio": ratio,
    }
)
```

:::

The ratio is `r round(ratio[1], 4)` at every rate,
which is the ratio of the products of factorials,
$\paren{5!}^3 / \paren{6! \, 5! \, 4!}$.
:::
